after.summary: In 1959, one of the most significant events of the Khrushchev Thaw took place in Moscow’s Sokolniki Park: the American National Exhibition. In its pavilions, Soviet citizens could explore American art and see how Americans lived: what cars they drove, what kitchens they cooked in, and what beds they slept in. But what the exhibition in Sokolniki is remembered for most is not its works of art and design, but the “Kitchen Debate.” On July 24, U.S. Vice President Richard Nixon arrived for the exhibition’s opening and met with Soviet Communist Party First Secretary Nikita Khrushchev. Together, the two toured a model American house that, according to its creators, any U.S. citizen could afford. When the two politicians stepped into the kitchen, Khrushchev had to make the case for the Soviet system while surrounded by unprecedented marvels: a refrigerator, a washing machine, and a dishwasher. Architecture journalist Asya Zolnikova tells the story of what that American house looked like, what else was at the Sokolniki exhibition, and what impact it had on U.S.-Russian relations.
